Chapter 3: Coming of Age and Confronting Race
You know, adolescence is one of those times when everything feels more intense—like the world’s edges are sharper, and the big questions you could once ignore suddenly demand your attention.
Imagine being a teenager in Hawaii during these years. Every day, stepping into school meant entering a world that was its own tiny version of society—with its unwritten rules and invisible boundaries. Friend groups came together over what they had in common, but there were always those subtle reminders that not everyone saw things the same way. Sometimes it was just a joke. Sometimes, just a quick glance. And in those moments, the young man couldn’t help but notice where he fit in—and where he didn’t.
He found himself drifting between different circles, never really feeling fully at home in any one. So, he learned to adapt. He’d watch, listen, and figure out what people expected from him.
But life outside school wasn’t exactly easier. There were the usual teenage temptations and distractions, those restless urges to rebel or the doubts that kept him up at night. Like a lot of young people, he tried on different versions of himself—testing out new attitudes, changing the way he talked, even shifting his beliefs, just to see what fit. It was so easy to fall into sarcasm, or to use humor as armor, hiding what he really felt from everyone else. Underneath, though, those big questions about who he was and where he belonged kept bubbling up.
One thing that really stood out during this time was the absence of his father. He wondered what kind of advice he was missing, what lessons he might’ve learned if his dad wasn’t so far away. His mom, as caring and supportive as she was, couldn’t fully grasp what it meant to be a biracial teenager in a world that always seemed to want simple answers to complicated questions.
Still, it wasn’t all struggle. There were bright moments too—a teacher believing in him, a friend having his back—those little flashes of acceptance that made all the difference. It started to become clear that identity wasn’t just about how other people saw him, but about the choices he made and the values he decided to live by. And as he looked around, he realized that trying to figure out who you are isn’t just his story—it’s something everyone goes through, shaped by where we come from, but not defined by it.
Moving on from high school into college, his world got even bigger. He dove into books about the civil rights movement, read about people who’d struggled and triumphed before him. That’s when it hit him—the questions he was facing weren’t only his own. They were part of this much larger story, one that was still unfolding. And with that came both comfort and a sense of responsibility. He saw that his journey was linked to something greater than himself.
Growing up, he learned, isn’t a straight path. It’s more like a zigzag—steps forward, steps back. Sometimes everything’s crystal clear, and other times the way ahead just disappears. But through it all, he started to see that confronting race wasn’t just about making sense of the world. It was about making sense of himself.
So, here’s the real takeaway: searching for identity isn’t about reaching some final answer. It’s a lifelong process. One that asks for honesty, courage, and the willingness to look at truths that aren’t always easy to face.
